title: The tangent-two-theta theorem
subtitle: G2 lecture 117000 · baseline companion · needs expansion
adaptation: First-pass source-derived outline. Section excerpts and any vector equation come from the spoken lecture and its display-only mathematics appendix. Expand with worked mathematics, proofs and topic-specific diagrams.

slides.title: The problem and its setting
slides.lead: The sine-two-theta theorem controls an operator that vanishes both at zero angle and at ninety degrees.
body: To recover a stronger geometric conclusion, we need to know which branch of that function we occupy. For a self-adjoint operator with an ordered two-block gap, an off-diagonal perturbation gives us exactly that information. The selected upper spectral subspace remains at angles strictly less than forty-five degrees from the original upper subspace. On that branch, the tangent of twice the angle is finite and can be controlled sharply.

slides.title: State the strong hypotheses
slides.lead: Let T be self-adjoint on a finite-dimensional Hilbert space H.
body: Let U reduce T. Assume the quadratic form of T on U is at least b times squared length, and its form on U perpendicular is at most a times squared length, with b greater than a. Write delta for b minus a. Perturb T by a self-adjoint operator H zero whose diagonal compressions onto U and onto U perpendicular both vanish. Denote the new operator by S. Let V be the upper reducing subspace selected from S. To make the theorem precise, assume the quadratic form of S on V is at least b, and on V perpendicular at most a.

slides.title: Derive the exact planar formula
slides.lead: Take T diagonal with entries b and a, where b is greater than a.
body: Let the perturbation H zero have zero diagonal and off-diagonal entries h. Then S has rows b, h and h, a. Consider an eigenvector for the upper eigenvalue, making an angle theta from the first coordinate axis. To diagonalize S, use an ordinary plane rotation. The off-diagonal entry in the rotated matrix is h times cosine twice theta minus half of b minus a times sine twice theta, with the sign depending on the orientation of the rotation. Setting that entry equal to zero gives tangent twice theta equal to two h divided by delta, with an appropriate choice of oriented theta.

slides.title: How do we know the upper space stays on the correct branch?
slides.lead: We need a reason that does not depend on diagonalizing a two-by-two matrix.
body: Let P be projection onto U and let J equal twice P minus the identity. Center T at the midpoint c of a and b. The form-gap hypothesis gives a coercive inequality: the real part of the inner product of J times T minus c with x is at least half delta times the squared norm of x. Because the perturbation is off-diagonal, J H zero is skew-adjoint. Its quadratic form has zero real part. So the same coercive lower bound holds with S in place of T. This bound first proves spectral repulsion: no eigenvector of S can have an eigenvalue in the open gap.

slides.title: Derive the sharp graph inequality
slides.lead: Represent V as the graph of an operator Z from U into U perpendicular.
body: The strict branch conclusion gives operator norm Z less than one. Its singular values are tangents of the principal angles. Relative to U plus U perpendicular, write T as diagonal blocks A plus and A minus. Write the off-diagonal perturbation using K and K adjoint. Thus S has upper-right block K adjoint and lower-left block K. A graph vector has components u and Z u. The condition that its image under S remains on the graph yields a Riccati equation. In words: K plus A minus Z equals Z A plus plus Z K adjoint Z. This equation contains both linear Sylvester terms and a quadratic correction from the off-diagonal coupling.

slides.title: Interpret the cosine denominator
slides.lead: The difference between the doubled sine and doubled tangent is the denominator cosine twice theta.
body: For angles below forty-five degrees, cosine twice theta is positive. We can therefore pass from a bound on sine twice theta to a bound on tangent twice theta only if we can control that denominator. The off-diagonal spectral structure supplies the required positivity, and the graph argument obtains the sharp quantitative comparison. At forty-five degrees the denominator vanishes. The theorem says that no finite off-diagonal perturbation satisfying its hypotheses reaches that angle. A family can approach it as the coupling grows, but never attain it at finite size.

slides.title: Compare the two double-angle theorems
slides.lead: The sine-two-theta theorem needs a two-block gap for T and reducing subspaces for T and S.
body: It allows a general self-adjoint perturbation and gives delta times a doubled-sine norm at most twice the perturbation norm. The tangent-two-theta theorem adds off-diagonality, matching upper and lower spectral bounds for the selected perturbed subspace, and an operator-norm control. It gives both an angle strictly below forty-five degrees and the sharp doubled-tangent inequality. The stronger conclusion costs stronger hypotheses. It cannot be obtained simply by dividing the sine estimate by cosine twice theta without proving the branch and controlling that cosine.

slides.title: A final numerical check
slides.lead: Let delta equal two and let the coupling h equal one.
body: The formula gives tangent twice theta equal one, so theta is twenty-two point five degrees. Then cosine twice theta and sine twice theta both equal the square root of two divided by two. The sine-two-theta estimate gives two times approximately zero point seven zero seven at most two. The tangent-two-theta estimate gives two times one at most two, with equality. As h increases to ten, tangent twice theta equals ten and theta approaches forty-five degrees from below. The doubled sine becomes close to one, while the doubled tangent records the increasing difficulty of maintaining a graph with slope below one.

slides.title: What to retain
slides.lead: The spectral branch proof establishes that the cosine of twice every relevant angle is positive; the Riccati estimate then controls its reciprocal effect quantitatively.
